claim: About half of the eukaryotic genome can be transcribed into RNA in an individual cell.
source: The complex genome of eukaryotes is pervasively transcribed and efforts to comprehensively define all transcripts have led to the idea that about half of the genome can be transcribed into RNA in an individual cell (Djebali et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Djebali et al., 2012

claim: GENCODE lists 17,957 lncRNA genes in the human genome.
source: current and careful curation projects, such as the GENCODE and FANTOM projects, list 17,957 and 27,919 lncRNA genes, respectively (Figure 1A), in their most recent data releases of the human genome (Frankish et al., 2019; Hon et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Frankish et al., 2019 and reference to Figure 1A

claim: FANTOM lists 27,919 lncRNA genes in the human genome.
source: current and careful curation projects, such as the GENCODE and FANTOM projects, list 17,957 and 27,919 lncRNA genes, respectively (Figure 1A), in their most recent data releases of the human genome (Frankish et al., 2019; Hon et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hon et al., 2017 and reference to Figure 1A

claim: The number of lncRNA genes is in the same range or higher than the number of protein-coding genes (19,954).
source: Hence, the number of lncRNA genes are in the same range, or even a bit higher, than the number of PCGs (19,954).
evidence: Based on comparison of lncRNA gene counts to PCG counts from GENCODE data

claim: Most lncRNAs are transcribed by RNA polymerase 2 (POL II).
source: Like PCGs, most lncRNAs are transcribed by POL II (RNA polymerase 2, a multiprotein complex), but are more tissue-specific compared to PCGs (for review see Ransohoff et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to review by Ransohoff et al., 2018

claim: LncRNAs are more tissue-specific compared to protein-coding genes.
source: Like PCGs, most lncRNAs are transcribed by POL II (RNA polymerase 2, a multiprotein complex), but are more tissue-specific compared to PCGs (for review see Ransohoff et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to review by Ransohoff et al., 2018

claim: LncRNA promoters have fewer overlapping transcription factor binding motifs compared to protein-coding gene promoters.
source: Both biotypes (PCGs and lncRNAs) have conserved core promoter sequences with fewer overlapping TF binding motifs in lncRNA promoters, resulting in an overall lower expression level compared to PCGs (Figure 2; Mattioli et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mattioli et al., 2019 and reference to Figure 2

claim: LncRNAs have an overall lower expression level compared to protein-coding genes.
source: Both biotypes (PCGs and lncRNAs) have conserved core promoter sequences with fewer overlapping TF binding motifs in lncRNA promoters, resulting in an overall lower expression level compared to PCGs (Figure 2; Mattioli et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mattioli et al., 2019 and reference to Figure 2

claim: The architecture of the core promoter defines the degree of lncRNA expression.
source: Thus, the architecture of the core promoter is the first player that defines the degree of lncRNA expression (Batut and Gingeras, 2017; Mattioli et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Batut and Gingeras, 2017 and Mattioli et al., 2019

claim: Many lncRNAs can be generated from enhancer elements.
source: Many lncRNAs can also be generated from such enhancer elements, which contributes to their overall more tissue-specific expression when compared to PCGs (Mattioli et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mattioli et al., 2019

claim: The splicing efficiency of lncRNAs is lower than protein-coding genes.
source: The mechanism of PCG and lncRNA splicing is similar, although the splicing efficiency of lncRNAs is lower than PCGs, likely due to the loss of proximal RNA POL II phosphorylation over 5' splice sites (Krchnáková et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Krchnáková et al., 2019

claim: Lower splicing efficiency of lncRNAs is likely due to the loss of proximal RNA POL II phosphorylation over 5' splice sites.
source: The mechanism of PCG and lncRNA splicing is similar, although the splicing efficiency of lncRNAs is lower than PCGs, likely due to the loss of proximal RNA POL II phosphorylation over 5' splice sites (Krchnáková et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Krchnáková et al., 2019, with speculative language 'likely due to'

claim: LncRNAs show signs of co-transcriptional cleavage and premature termination with Thr4p PolII enriched over the entire lncRNA body.
source: In addition, lncRNAs show signs of co-transcriptional cleavage and premature termination with Thr4p PolII enriched over the entire lncRNA body (Schlackow et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schlackow et al., 2017

claim: In humans, there are 569,005 elements that meet the criterion of a polyadenylation signal.
source: In humans, one can find 569,005 elements that meet the criterion of a pA signal (301,001 in mouse and 20,931 in C. elegans) (Herrmann et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Herrmann et al., 2020

claim: In mouse, there are 301,001 elements that meet the criterion of a polyadenylation signal.
source: In humans, one can find 569,005 elements that meet the criterion of a pA signal (301,001 in mouse and 20,931 in C. elegans) (Herrmann et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Herrmann et al., 2020

claim: In C. elegans, there are 20,931 elements that meet the criterion of a polyadenylation signal.
source: In humans, one can find 569,005 elements that meet the criterion of a pA signal (301,001 in mouse and 20,931 in C. elegans) (Herrmann et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Herrmann et al., 2020

claim: Transposable elements make up more than 44% of the human genome.
source: These mobile genomic elements make up more than 44% of the human genome (Lander et al., 2001) and attracted attention as important regulators of gene and genome activity (Bourque et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lander et al., 2001

claim: Approximately 75% of lncRNA transcripts contain sequence elements from transposable elements.
source: Approximately, 75% of lncRNA transcripts contain sequence elements from TEs (Kapusta et al., 2013) and some of them represent important sequence elements to direct lncRNA localization (Lubelsky and Ulitsky, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kapusta et al., 2013

claim: Some transposable elements represent important sequence elements to direct lncRNA localization.
source: Approximately, 75% of lncRNA transcripts contain sequence elements from TEs (Kapusta et al., 2013) and some of them represent important sequence elements to direct lncRNA localization (Lubelsky and Ulitsky, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lubelsky and Ulitsky, 2018

claim: 25% of transposable elements overlap with transcriptional start sites and polyadenylation signals of lncRNA genes.
source: In addition, 25% of TEs are found to overlap with TSS and pA signals of lncRNA genes (Kapusta et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kapusta et al., 2013

claim: XACT lncRNA protects the active X chromosome from being silenced.
source: One recent example is the primate-specific lncRNA XACT (Table 1), which has been shown to protect the active X chromosome from being silenced (antagonizing XIST lncRNA effect) and whose sequence contains elements derived from a TE (Casanova et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Casanova et al., 2019

claim: XACT lncRNA sequence contains elements derived from a transposable element.
source: One recent example is the primate-specific lncRNA XACT (Table 1), which has been shown to protect the active X chromosome from being silenced (antagonizing XIST lncRNA effect) and whose sequence contains elements derived from a TE (Casanova et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Casanova et al., 2019

claim: XACT lncRNA is regulated by a transposable element-derived enhancer element that harbors pioneer pluripotency factor binding sites.
source: Interestingly, XACT lncRNA is also regulated by a TE-derived enhancer element that harbors pioneer pluripotency factor binding sites.
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text without specific citation for this particular claim

claim: RNAs originating from non-coding genes associate with ribosomes.
source: It was already found some time ago that RNAs originating from NCGs do actually associate with ribosomes, the machinery that translates mRNAs into proteins (Ingolia et al., 2011; van Heesch et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ingolia et al., 2011 and van Heesch et al., 2014

claim: Some lncRNAs produce functional peptides.
source: In more recent in-depth studies, it was found that some lncRNAs do produce peptides and that some of these peptides are even functional (Chen et al., 2020; Ji et al., 2015; van Heesch et al., 2019), including within 5' and 3' untranslated regions (UTR) of mRNAs.
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen et al., 2020; Ji et al., 2015; van Heesch et al., 2019

claim: Capture Long Sequence (CLS) technology can precisely determine 5' and 3' ends and all splice variants of a transcript.
source: The advantage of this technology is the capability to precisely determine 5' and 3' ends and, ideally, all splice variants of a transcript.
evidence: Stated as an advantage of the CLS technology described in the manuscript

claim: The estimated mean number of exons per lncRNA using CLS was 4.27 compared to 3.59 measured by short-reads RNA-seq method.
source: For example, the estimated mean number of exons per lncRNA using CLS was 4.27 compared to 3.59 measured by short-reads RNA-seq method (Lagarde et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lagarde et al., 2017

claim: The Haunt lncRNA RNA is required for negative regulation of HoxA.
source: One interesting lncRNA gene example that reflects the duality of lncRNA genes with respect to their RNA-based mechanism on one side, and an enhancer element on the other side, is Haunt. While the RNA of Haunt is thought to be required for negative regulation of HoxA, the Haunt locus contains regulatory elements to activate the HoxA locus during in vitro differentiation of pluripotent stem cells (Yin et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yin et al., 2015

claim: The Haunt locus contains regulatory elements to activate the HoxA locus during in vitro differentiation of pluripotent stem cells.
source: One interesting lncRNA gene example that reflects the duality of lncRNA genes with respect to their RNA-based mechanism on one side, and an enhancer element on the other side, is Haunt. While the RNA of Haunt is thought to be required for negative regulation of HoxA, the Haunt locus contains regulatory elements to activate the HoxA locus during in vitro differentiation of pluripotent stem cells (Yin et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yin et al., 2015

claim: Deletion of the entire Lockd locus leads to a reduction of Cdkn1b expression.
source: The deletion of the entire locus of Lockd, including TSS upstream elements, leads to a reduction of Cdkn1b expression (Paralkar et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Paralkar et al., 2016

claim: The 5' genomic region of Lockd interacts genomically with the promoter of Cdkn1b.
source: While the 5' genomic region of Lockd interacts genomically with the promoter of Cdkn1b, this interaction is not altered if the transcription of Lockd is depleted by a pA signal inserted into the first exon of Lockd.
evidence: Stated in the manuscript based on the Lockd study

claim: The genomic locus of Lockd is important as a regulatory element rather than its transcriptional activity.
source: Thus, the genomic locus itself is important as an regulatory element rather than its transcriptional activity.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results described for Lockd

claim: The TSS of the Meteor lncRNA locus is important to license its cis-located gene Eomes for activation in the mesendoderm.
source: The TSS of the Meteor lncRNA locus is important to license its cis-located gene Eomes for activation in the mesendoderm (Alexanian et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Alexanian et al., 2017

claim: Lack of Meteor expression by TSS deletion causes the loss of Eomes activation during mesendoderm differentiation of mouse ESCs.
source: The lack of Meteor expression by TSS deletion causes the loss of Eomes activation during mesendoderm differentiation of mouse ESCs.
evidence: Stated in the manuscript based on Meteor study

claim: Decreasing levels of Meteor RNA during mesendoderm differentiation did not alter expression of downstream genes.
source: Decreasing levels of Meteor RNA during this process did not alter expression of downstream genes, arguing against an RNA-based function of Meteor.
evidence: Stated in the manuscript based on Meteor study

claim: Transcriptional inhibition of Meteor using a polyadenylation element insertion downstream of the Meteor TSS does not cause the Eomes gene to be silenced during mesendoderm differentiation.
source: Moreover, transcriptional inhibition of Meteor using a polyadenylation element insertion downstream of the Meteor TSS does not cause the Eomes gene to be silenced during mesendoderm differentiation (Alexanian et al., 2017; Engreitz et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Alexanian et al., 2017 and Engreitz et al., 2016

claim: The genomic locus Meteor harbors important regulatory elements to render the cis-located Eomes gene activatable during differentiation.
source: This finding argues against a transcription-based mechanism of Meteor and suggests that the genomic locus Meteor harbors important regulatory elements to render the cis-located Eomes gene activatable during differentiation.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results described for Meteor

claim: Transcription of ThymoD prevents methylation of a CTCF-binding site located within its transcriptional unit.
source: An excellent example of a lncRNA with a defined regulatory element within transcription unit is the ThymoD lncRNA locus. Its transcription prevents methylation of a CTCF-binding site located within its transcriptional unit (Isoda et al., 2017; Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by citation to Isoda et al., 2017 and reference to Figure 3A

claim: CTCF binding at ThymoD allows looping of the Bcl11b transcription unit in the same domain as activating regions of Bcl11b.
source: The binding of CTCF allows looping of the Bcl11b transcription unit in the same domain as activating regions of Bcl11b.
evidence: Stated in the manuscript based on ThymoD study

claim: When transcription of ThymoD is blocked by insertion of a pA signal after exon two, the CTCF-binding site is methylated and Bcl11b activation is lost.
source: This activation is lost when the transcription of ThymoD is blocked by insertion of a pA signal after exon two and before the CTCF-binding site and, consequentially, the CTCF-binding site is methylated (Figure 3A).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript with reference to Figure 3A

claim: The ThymoD RNA is dispensable for Bcl11b regulation.
source: Therefore, the transcriptional activity has an indirect, structural effect on the regulation of Bcl11b while the ThymoD RNA is dispensable.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results described for ThymoD

claim: The Protocadherin alpha cluster produces three distinct variants from three alternative TSSs to achieve stochastic expression of splice variants.
source: The cluster of Pcdhα produces three distinct variants from three alternative TSSs to achieve stochastic expression of splice variants from this cluster.
evidence: Stated in the manuscript based on Pcdhα study

claim: The first exon of each Protocadherin alpha variant contains an antisense lncRNA transcript (Pcdhα-as).
source: The first exon of each of these variants contains an antisense lncRNA transcript (Pcdhα-as) (Canzio et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Canzio et al., 2019

claim: Expression of Pcdhα lncRNAs precedes the expression of the protein-coding genes.
source: The expression of the lncRNAs precedes the expression of the PCGs and positively regulates the most nearby PCG expression.
evidence: Stated in the manuscript based on Pcdhα study

claim: Expression of Pcdhα-as variants leads to demethylation of a CTCF-binding site upstream of the Pcdhα protein-coding gene.
source: Expression of the Pcdhα-as variants leads to the demethylation of a CTCF-binding site in the region upstream of the Pcdhα PCG, thereby allowing for a stable loop formation with the distal enhancer region and a positive effect on the PCGs expression.
evidence: Stated in the manuscript based on Pcdhα study

claim: Under 0% galactose, the transcription factor Reb1 binds to the promoter region of GAL10-ncRNA and fully activates its expression.
source: Under 0% galactose, the TF Reb1 binds to the promoter region of GAL10-ncRNA antisense to GAL10 and fully activates its expression (Houseley et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Houseley et al., 2008

claim: The transcriptional unit of GAL10-ncRNA overlaps with the TSS of GAL10 and GAL1, leading to inhibition of these genes.
source: The transcriptional unit of GAL10-ncRNA overlaps with the TSS of GAL10 and GAL1, leading to inhibition of the GAL10 and GAL1 gene by promoting high levels of H3K36me3 methylation and hypoacetylation at the GAL10 and GAL1 promoters.
evidence: Stated in the manuscript based on GAL10-ncRNA study

claim: Addition of galactose blocks GAL10-ncRNA expression and causes hyperacetylation of the GAL10 and GAL1 promoters.
source: Addition of galactose to the growth medium blocks GAL10-ncRNA expression and hyperacetylation of the GAL10 and GAL1 promoters, leading to expression of genes that encode galactose fermenting proteins (Figure 3B).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript with reference to Figure 3B

claim: The TSS of AIRN lncRNA is located in the second intron of the Igf2r protein-coding gene.
source: The TSS of the lncRNA AIRN is located in the second intron of the Igf2r PCG and AIRN is transcribed antisense to Ifg2r.
evidence: Stated in the manuscript based on AIRN study

claim: Transcription of AIRN negatively regulates Igfr2.
source: Transcription of AIRN negatively regulates Igfr2 (Santoro et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Santoro et al., 2013

claim: When transcription of AIRN is blocked by a polyA insertion before the promoter of Igf2r, negative regulation of Igf2r is abolished.
source: When transcription of AIRN is blocked by a polyA insertion before the promoter of Igf2r, this negative regulation is abolished (Figure 3B).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript with reference to Figure 3B

claim: If a polyA is inserted after the promotor of Igf2r, the negative regulatory effect of AIRN on Igf2r is not observed.
source: However, if the same pA is inserted after the promotor of Igf2r, this negative regulatory effect on Igf2r is not observed (Latos et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Latos et al., 2012

claim: Upperhand is divergently expressed from the Hand2 protein-coding gene.
source: A lncRNA gene transcription that influences an enhancer is Upperhand, which is divergently expressed from the Hand2 protein-coding gene (Anderson et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Anderson et al., 2016

claim: Loss of Upperhand transcription leads to a loss of histone acetylation upstream of Hand2, including at the cardiac enhancer.
source: Loss of Upperhand transcription leads to a loss of histone acetylation upstream of Hand2, including at the cardiac enhancer.
evidence: Stated in the manuscript based on Upperhand study

claim: Loss of Upperhand transcription reduces binding of GATA4 to the Hand2 cardiac enhancer.
source: As a result, binding of GATA4 to its previously defined enhancer (McFadden et al., 2000) is reduced, and Hand2 expression in the heart is reduced as well.
evidence: Stated in the manuscript with citation to McFadden et al., 2000 for the enhancer definition

claim: A complete deletion of the Upperhand transcription unit causes loss of Hand2 5'UTR expression.
source: A complete deletion of the Upperhand transcription unit that encompasses all known regulatory regions of the Hand2 gene as well, causes loss of Hand2 5'UTR expression (Han et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Han et al., 2019

claim: A promoter deletion of Upperhand causes a loss of its RNA but has no effect on Hand2 expression.
source: However, a promoter deletion of Upperhand causes a loss of its RNA while leaving all other elements in that region intact, but no effect on Hand2 expression was observed in this case.
evidence: Stated in the manuscript based on Upperhand study

claim: A deletion of the last two exons from Upperhand has a slight effect on Hand2 expression.
source: Furthermore, a deletion of the last two exons from Upperhand has a slight effect on Hand2 expression.
evidence: Stated in the manuscript based on Upperhand study

claim: The Upperhand RNA generates peptides that might be functional.
source: In addition, although the Upperhand RNA is suggested to be not required for its in vivo function, the RNA generates peptides that might be functional (van Heesch et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to van Heesch et al., 2019, with speculative language 'might be functional'

claim: The Ftx locus is found 140 kb upstream of Xist.
source: The XIST lncRNA locus is flanked by many lncRNAs, and one of them is the Ftx locus found 140 kb upstream of Xist (Chureau et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chureau et al., 2002

claim: The transcription of Ftx, and not the produced RNA, is important to regulate Xist.
source: However, detailed analysis uncovered that the transcription of Ftx, and not the produced RNA, is important to regulate Xist (Furlan et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Furlan et al., 2018

claim: Knockdown of Ftx RNA does not cause a loss of Xist expression.
source: Knockdown of Ftx RNA does not cause a loss of Xist expression, but deletion of the promoter of Ftx, and the consequential loss of Ftx transcription, causes the loss of Xist expression.
evidence: Stated in the manuscript based on Ftx study

claim: Deletion of the promoter of Ftx causes the loss of Xist expression.
source: Knockdown of Ftx RNA does not cause a loss of Xist expression, but deletion of the promoter of Ftx, and the consequential loss of Ftx transcription, causes the loss of Xist expression.
evidence: Stated in the manuscript based on Ftx study

claim: CRISPRi of Ftx causes loss of Xist expression.
source: CRISPRi of Ftx similarly causes loss of Xist expression, suggesting that transcription of Ftx is the positive regulator of Xist expression.
evidence: Stated in the manuscript based on Ftx study

claim: The promoter of Xist and Ftx are flanked by CTCF-occupied sites.
source: Strikingly, the promoter of Xist and Ftx are flanked by CTCF-occupied sites.
evidence: Stated in the manuscript based on Ftx study

claim: Deleting the CTCF-binding sites at the Ftx promoter has no effect on the expression level of Xist.
source: However, deleting the CTCF-binding sites alone at the Ftx promoter has no effect on the expression level of Xist, arguing that genome folding induced by Ftx activity does not involve CTCF-binding.
evidence: Stated in the manuscript based on Ftx study

claim: The Chaserr lncRNA locus lies 16 kb upstream of the Chd2 protein-coding gene.
source: Another good example is the Chaserr lncRNA locus, which lies 16 kb upstream of the Chd2 protein- coding gene (Rom et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rom et al., 2019

claim: Knock-down of Chaserr RNA causes a slight increase in Chd2 expression.
source: Although, knock-down of Chaserr RNA does cause a slight increase in Chd2 expression, additional lines of evidence infer that the transcription of the lncRNA gene is likely the most important function of Chaserr in regulating Chd2 (Figure 4).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript with reference to Figure 4

claim: The promoter of Chaserr interacts with the Chd2 promoter in chromosome conformation capture analysis.
source: In addition, the promoter of Chaserr interacts with the Chd2 promoter in chromosome conformation capture analysis.
evidence: Stated in the manuscript based on Chaserr study

claim: Upon deletion of the Chaserr promoter region, the Chd2 promoter increasingly interacts with other enhancer elements upstream.
source: Upon deletion of the Chaserr promoter region, the Chd2 promoter increasingly interacts with other enhancer elements upstream.
evidence: Stated in the manuscript based on Chaserr study

claim: If the gene body of Chaserr is deleted while leaving the promoter intact, changes in enhancer/Chd2-promoter contacts are not observed.
source: In contrast, if the gene body of Chaserr is deleted, leaving the promoter intact, these changes in enhancer/Chd2-promoter contacts are not observed.
evidence: Stated in the manuscript based on Chaserr study

claim: The transcription initiation activity of Chaserr rather than transcription elongation is important for regulation of Chd2.
source: A plausible explanation is that the transcription initiation activity rather than the transcription elongation is important for regulation of Chd2 by Chaserr.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results described for Chaserr, with speculative language 'plausible explanation'

claim: PVT1 lncRNA was originally discovered as a genomic translocation that causes the activation of the Myc oncogene.
source: The Pvt-1 lncRNA was originally discovered as a genomic translocation that causes the activation of the Myc oncogene (Adams and Cory, 1985).
evidence: Supported by citation to Adams and Cory, 1985

claim: MiRNAs embedded in the lncRNA transcript of PVT1 are important for regulation of target genes.
source: Initially, it was suggested that miRNAs embedded in the lncRNA transcript of PVT1 are important for regulation of target genes (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2019

claim: The activity of PVT1's major TSS serves as a boundary element to shield the MYC promoter from over-activation by an enhancer located within the transcriptional unit of PVT1.
source: The activity of its major TSS serves as a boundary element to shield the MYC promoter from over-activation by an enhancer located within the transcriptional unit of PVT1 (Cho et al., 2018; Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cho et al., 2018 and reference to Figure 4

claim: The transcriptional activity of PVT1 is important for its shielding capacity, but not the elongation of the transcription.
source: The transcriptional activity is important for this shielding capacity, but not the elongation of the transcription (Figure 4).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript with reference to Figure 4

claim: Handsdown is most significantly expressed in the developing heart.
source: The Handsdown locus is expressed in the same tissues as Hand2 but is most significantly expressed in the developing heart.
evidence: Stated in the manuscript based on Handsdown study

claim: Transcription of Handsdown is important to negatively regulate the expression of Hand2.
source: We have shown that transcription of Handsdown is important to negatively regulate the expression of Hand2 (Figure 4).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript with reference to Figure 4

claim: HAND2 transcription factor binds two distinct sites around the TSS of Handsdown in the developing E9.5 heart.
source: Moreover, the HAND2 TF binds two distinct sites around the TSS of Handsdown in the developing E9.5 heart (Laurent et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Laurent et al., 2017

claim: HAND2 activates its own suppressor region (Handsdown) in a negative feedback loop to control its dosage.
source: This suggests that HAND2 activates its own suppressor region in a negative feedback loop to control its dosage.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results described for Handsdown, with speculative language 'suggests'

claim: Deletion of the TSS region of Handsdown does not result in the expected upregulation of Hand2.
source: However, deletion of the TSS region of Handsdown, including only one of the HAND2 occupied sites, does not result in the expected upregulation of Hand2 (George et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to George et al., 2019

claim: Deletion of one or the major TSS of Handsdown can lead to the appearance of alternate transcripts.
source: Multiple, potential TSS regions are present in at the 5' region of Handsdown and the deletion of one or the major TSS can lead to the appearance of alternate transcripts (Lavalou et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lavalou et al., 2019

claim: Loss of one copy of the Hand2 gene causes malformations during development.
source: The dosage of Hand2 is particularly important as loss of one copy of the Hand2 gene, as well as the gain of an additional copy of the Hand2 gene, causes malformations during development (Tamura et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tamura et al., 2014

claim: Gain of an additional copy of the Hand2 gene causes malformations during development.
source: The dosage of Hand2 is particularly important as loss of one copy of the Hand2 gene, as well as the gain of an additional copy of the Hand2 gene, causes malformations during development (Tamura et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tamura et al., 2014

claim: CTCF binding frequently co-localizes and interacts with the cohesin complex at TAD borders.
source: CTCF binding frequently co-localizes and interacts with the cohesin complex at TAD borders (Li et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2020

claim: Elimination of cohesin dissolves all chromatin TADs even in the presence of CTCF.
source: Indeed, elimination of cohesin dissolves all chromatin TADs even in the presence of CTCF (Rao et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rao et al., 2017

claim: Disruption of TADs by removal of CTCF or cohesin results in unexpected mild effects on gene expression.
source: Interestingly, disruption of the TADs either by removal of CTCF or cohesin results in unexpected mild effects on gene expression (Nora et al., 2017; Rao et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nora et al., 2017 and Rao et al., 2017

claim: The process of transcription can assist in reorganizing chromatin marks.
source: The process of transcription can assist in reorganizing chromatin marks (van Steensel and Furlong, 2019), allowing regions to be accessible for other factors or prevent others by diverting/directing the transcription machinery to nearby genes.
evidence: Supported by citation to van Steensel and Furlong, 2019

claim: ASOs that target the 5' end of an RNA can cleave nascent RNA during transcription.
source: Several recent publications demonstrate that ASOs that target the 5' end of an RNA can do this even on nascent RNA that is in the process of being transcribed (Eaton et al., 2020; Lai et al., 2020; Lee and Mendell, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Eaton et al., 2020; Lai et al., 2020; Lee and Mendell, 2020

claim: Premature cleavage of RNA by 5' ASOs leads to recruitment of XRN2 and employs the torpedo mechanism to evict the POL II transcription machinery prematurely.
source: This premature cleavage of RNA leads to the recruitment of XRN2 and employs the torpedo mechanism to evict the POL II transcription machinery prematurely.
evidence: Stated in the manuscript based on recent ASO studies

claim: To validate an RNA-based mechanism by ASOs, it is preferred to target the 3' end of the RNA-of-interest.
source: To validate an RNA-based mechanism by ASOs, it is preferred to target the 3' end of the RNA-of-interest.
evidence: Stated as a recommendation based on the understanding of ASO mechanisms

claim: Deletion of the entire transcription unit of a lncRNA locus will allow determination if the locus is functional.
source: With CRISPR/Cas9 deletions even in the mega-base range being feasible, the deletion of the entire transcription unit will allow one to determine if a lncRNA locus is functional at all (Barutcu et al., 2018; Kraft et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barutcu et al., 2018 and Kraft et al., 2015

claim: If removal of a complete lncRNA locus does not result in effects on gene expression, this locus can be marked non-functional in the analyzed biological system.
source: Simply put: if the removal of a complete lncRNA locus does not result in even subtle effects on gene expression, this locus can be marked non-functional, at least in the analyzed biological system.
evidence: Stated as a logical conclusion from experimental approach

claim: Removing a TSS might trigger the emergence of new transcripts from secondary TSS-like sites in the vicinity.
source: It has to be kept in mind, that removing a TSS might trigger the emergence of new transcripts from secondary TSS-like sites in the vicinity (Lavalou et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lavalou et al., 2019

claim: XIST acts via the produced RNA.
source: While XIST acts via the produced RNA (Brannan et al., 1990; Brown et al., 1992), the regulation of XIST, at least in part, does not.
evidence: Supported by citations to Brannan et al., 1990 and Brown et al., 1992

claim: Three major functional principles can be assigned to lncRNA loci: RNA as functional biomolecule, regulatory element embedded in transcription body, or process of transcription influences genome activity.
source: Currently, three major functional principles can be assigned to lncRNA loci (Figure 1B): (1) either the RNA is the functional biomolecule and interacts with other components in the cell, for example DNA, proteins or RNAs, (2) a gene regulatory element is embedded in the transcription body of a lncRNA gene and the activity of the lncRNA gene directs the activity of the regulatory element or (3) the process of transcription influences genome and thereby gene activity.
evidence: Stated in the manuscript with reference to Figure 1B

claim: The number of lncRNA genes was overestimated after their initial discovery.
source: While their number was overestimated after their initial discovery, similar to the overestimation of the number of PCGs at the beginning of the human genome project (Lander et al., 2001), current and careful curation projects, such as the GENCODE and FANTOM projects, list 17,957 and 27,919 lncRNA genes, respectively (Figure 1A), in their most recent data releases of the human genome (Frankish et al., 2019; Hon et al., 2017).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript with comparison to PCG overestimation
